title: Eurymedusa from Apeire; the 'gift of honour'
greek: Ἀπείρηθεν ... γέρας (Apeirēthen ... geras)
short: Nausicaa's old nurse was captured from the unknown land of Apeire and chosen as the king's geras, his special share of the spoil.
body: Apeire cannot be located; Merry calls it purely mythical, like Hypereia, and records the ancient glosses 'far-off land' or 'mainland' (ēpeiros). Its vagueness fits the Phaeacians' place outside ordinary geography; ironically, it shows that this peaceful people once took captives in raids, like any Homeric community. Eurymedusa was set aside as Alcinous' geras, the prize of honour given to a leader before the general division of booty, the institution over which Akhilleus and Agamemnon quarrel in Iliad 1. Old nurses are important figures in the Odyssey: Eurycleia, bought by Laertes, nursed Odysseus and is the first to recognise him (19.386-475). The detail adds depth to the household before Odysseus enters it.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.8-10

anchor: cast about him a thick mist
title: The protective mist
greek: πολλὴν ἠέρα χεῦε (pollēn ēera cheue)
short: Athena wraps Odysseus in a thick mist (aēr) so that he walks unseen through the city; Virgil gave Aeneas the same protection at Carthage.
body: Homeric aēr is not 'air' in the later sense but haze or mist, which Merry explains 'served to make invisible those enveloped in it'. In the Iliad gods use it to snatch their favourites from battle (Il. 3.380-2, 20.444). Here its purpose is social: no Phaeacian should insult or question him before he reaches the queen. Athena's warning that the Phaeacians 'endure not stranger-folk' (7.32-3) sits oddly beside their later generosity, and critics have debated whether it reflects a real xenophobia (cf. Nausicaa's fear of gossip) or is simply part of Athena's protective plan. The mist dissolves at the dramatic moment when he clasps Arete's knees (7.143). Virgil imitates the scene closely: Venus surrounds Aeneas and Achates with mist as they walk into Carthage (Aeneid 1.411-14), and it parts when Aeneas reveals himself to Dido (1.586-8).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.15

title: Athena as a girl with a water-jar
greek: παρθενικῇ εἰκυῖα νεήνιδι, κάλπιν ἐχούσῃ (parthenikēi eikuia neēnidi, kalpin echousēi)
short: Athena meets Odysseus at the town's edge disguised as a young girl carrying a water-jar, the typical figure of an arrival scene.
body: Arrival scenes in the Odyssey often feature a girl at a spring or with water: Odysseus' scouts meet the daughter of the Laestrygonian king drawing water (10.105-11), and Athena meets Odysseus on Ithaca in the guise of a young shepherd (13.221-5). The type is familiar from other ancient traditions of a stranger meeting a woman at a well. The irony is deliberate: Odysseus asks his 'child' for directions, and the goddess plays the role perfectly, adding a description of Arete. Merry discusses whether parthenikē is an adjective or a noun in apposition. Athena's disguises in the Phaeacian books are always humble (a friend, a girl, a herald, a man at the games: 6.22, 8.8, 8.193), consistent with her reluctance to appear openly while Poseidon's anger lasts.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.20
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 7.19-20

title: Ships as swift as thought
greek: τῶν νέες ὠκεῖαι ὡς εἰ πτερὸν ἠὲ νόημα (tōn nees ōkeiai hōs ei pteron ēe noēma)
short: Phaeacian ships are 'swift as a wing or a thought', a first hint of their magical nature.
body: The comparison to thought (noēma) is the extreme of speed and anticipates the fuller description in Book VIII: the Phaeacian ships need no pilots or steering-oars, understand the minds of men and know every city (8.557-63), and travel to Euboea and back in a day (7.321-6). Merry comments on the compressed form of the simile. Homer elsewhere compares the speed of Hera's flight to the darting thought of a well-travelled man (Il. 15.80-3), and the Homeric Hymn to Hermes uses thought for the god's speed (43-6). The Phaeacians owe this gift to Poseidon, 'for this the Earth-shaker has granted them' (7.35), the same god whose resentment of their convoys will be their undoing.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.36

title: Arete and her family
greek: Ἀρήτη δ᾽ ὄνομ᾽ ἐστὶν ἐπώνυμον (Arētē d' onom' estin epōnumon)
short: The queen's name is Arete, 'prayed for'; she is Alcinous' niece as well as his wife, both descended from Poseidon through Nausithous.
body: Athena says the name is epōnumon, 'aptly given'. Homer probably connects Arētē with arētos, 'prayed for' (from araomai), as a longed-for only child; it should not be confused with aretē, 'excellence', which has a short e, though the pun has often been noticed. The genealogy (7.56-66) runs from Poseidon and Periboea, daughter of Eurymedon king of the Giants, to Nausithous, whose sons were Rhexenor and Alcinous. Rhexenor died young, killed by Apollo 'a bridegroom though he was' (Merry: 'before his bridal days were over'), leaving only Arete, whom her uncle married. Ancient scholia report that Hesiod made Arete Alcinous' sister rather than his niece. Uncle-niece marriage keeps the inheritance within the royal line, which may be the point.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.54, 7.56-66

title: Eurymedon and the Giants
greek: ὑπερθύμοισι Γιγάντεσσιν (huperthumoisi Gigantessin)
short: The Phaeacian royal line descends through Periboea from Eurymedon, king of the Giants, who destroyed his reckless people and himself.
body: Homer's Giants are a mortal (or semi-divine) race of arrogant men, not yet the monsters who storm heaven. Merry observes that Homer knows nothing of the Gigantomachia of later legend, the battle of gods and Giants of Hesiod's successors and Athenian art. They appear again as the Laestrygonians, 'not like men but like Giants' (10.120), and Alcinous puts them beside the Cyclopes as peoples near to the gods (7.205-6). The Phaeacians thus descend both from Poseidon and from a violent people destroyed by its own folly, a dark strand in their idyllic history that recalls the suitors, likewise 'reckless' and brought to ruin.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.59
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 7.58-60

anchor: as no other woman on earth
title: The honour of Arete
greek: καί μιν ἔτισ᾽ ὡς οὔ τις ἐπὶ χθονὶ τίεται ἄλλη (kai min etis' hōs ou tis epi chthoni tietai allē)
short: Arete is honoured by husband, children and people like a goddess, and her good sense even settles quarrels among men.
body: Few women in Homer receive such praise. Arete is greeted in the streets 'as a goddess', possesses 'good understanding' (noos esthlos), and 'makes an end of strife even among their husbands' for the women she favours, a judicial role normally reserved for kings (cf. the judge-king of 19.109-14). Merry comments on the grammar of 7.69 and cites parallels. In Book XI it is Arete who first speaks after Odysseus pauses in his tale, calls him 'my guest' and urges more gifts (11.335-41), though Echeneus tactfully notes that the final word rests with Alcinous (11.344-6). Scholars disagree on how much real power she has: some see a sign of a matrilineal or queen-centred society, others a poetic ideal of the wise wife and a foil to Penelope. Her careful silence and shrewd question (7.237-9) show her authority at work.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.69
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 7.53-77

title: Athena goes to Marathon and Athens
greek: ἵκετο δ᾽ ἐς Μαραθῶνα καὶ εὐρυάγυιαν Ἀθήνην, / δῦνε δ᾽ Ἐρεχθῆος πυκινὸν δόμον (iketo d' es Marathōna kai euruaguian Athēnēn, / dune d' Erechthēos pukinon domon)
short: Leaving Scheria, Athena goes to her own city, Athens, and enters the house of Erechtheus, the shrine she shared with the hero-king.
body: Erechtheus was a legendary king of Athens, born from the earth and reared by Athena, who installed him in her temple (Il. 2.546-51). The 'strong house of Erechtheus' is, as Merry says, the temple on the Acropolis, the predecessor of the Erechtheion. Merry also reports the ancient suspicion that the lines were added by a later rhapsode to gratify Athenian feeling; Homer seldom refers to Athens, and the reference to Marathon is unique. Whether interpolated or not, the lines have a narrative function: Athena withdraws at the threshold of the palace, leaving Odysseus to win his welcome alone.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.80-1
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 7.80-1

title: The palace of Alcinous
greek: χάλκεον οὐδόν ... ὥς τε γὰρ ἠελίου αἴγλη πέλεν ἠὲ σελήνης (chalkeon oudon ... hōs te gar ēeliou aiglē pelen ēe selēnēs)
short: Before entering, Odysseus stands and gazes at a palace of bronze, gold and silver gleaming like the sun or moon, a fairy-tale building.
body: The description, the longest of a building in Homer, moves from the threshold through the hall to the orchards and springs, seen through Odysseus' wondering eyes (7.82-3, 133-4: 'he stood and gazed'). The line on the gleam of sun or moon also describes Menelaus' palace (4.45), but Alcinous' house outdoes it: bronze walls, golden doors, silver doorposts and lintel, magical animals, golden statues. Archaeologists have compared real Mycenaean palaces, with their decorated thresholds and blue friezes, but the overall effect is idealised, with Near Eastern parallels in its metalwork and magical guardians. It is the material image of the Phaeacians' near-divine existence: 'Such were the glorious gifts of the gods' (7.132).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.86-7
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 7.84-132

title: Kuanos: the blue frieze
greek: περὶ δὲ θριγκὸς κυάνοιο (peri de thrinkos kuanoio)
short: Kuanos is a dark-blue material, probably blue glass paste or enamel; the palace walls are topped with a blue frieze.
body: Murray transliterates the Greek as 'cyanus'. The word gives English 'cyan', and in Homer describes dark blue or black things: Zeus's brows, the hair of Hector, clouds. Merry admits that 'it is impossible to say with certainty' what the coping of kuanos was. Archaeology has supplied a probable answer: the palace at Tiryns had an alabaster frieze inlaid with blue glass paste, and a Mycenaean term for blue glass (ku-wa-no) appears in the Linear B tablets. Akhilleus' shield and Agamemnon's breastplate also have bands of kuanos (Il. 11.24, 18.564). The detail is one of several in Homer that preserve memories of Bronze Age luxury.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.86-7

title: The gold and silver watchdogs
greek: χρύσειοι δ᾽ ἑκάτερθε καὶ ἀργύρεοι κύνες ἦσαν (chruseioi d' hekaterthe kai argureoi kunes ēsan)
short: Hephaestus made gold and silver dogs, 'immortal and ageless', to guard Alcinous' palace: living statues or magical images.
body: Are they alive? Homer says they are 'immortal and ageless', the formula for divine beings, and that Hephaestus made them 'to guard' the house, which suggests real magical guardians like the golden maidservants who help Hephaestus walk (Il. 18.417-20). Merry, however, thought it improbable that the poet meant anything more than images of dogs and boys. Christopher Faraone has compared Near Eastern practices of burying apotropaic figures of dogs at doorways, and argued that the Homeric dogs reflect such magical protective statues. The ambiguity is part of the Phaeacian world's charm: art and life, craft and magic shade into each other.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.91
C. A. Faraone, 'Hephaestus the Magician and Near Eastern Parallels for Alcinous' Watchdogs', Greek, Roman and Byzantine Studies 28 (1987) 257-80

title: The golden torch-bearers
greek: χρύσειοι δ᾽ ἄρα κοῦροι ἐϋδμήτων ἐπὶ βωμῶν (chruseioi d' ara kouroi eudmētōn epi bōmōn)
short: Golden statues of youths stand on pedestals holding torches to light the night-time banquets; Lucretius borrowed them as a symbol of luxury.
body: Like the dogs, the golden youths blur the line between statue and servant. The word for pedestal, bōmos, is usually 'altar', so the figures stand on bases like votive statues. Lucretius took them over in his picture of the useless luxury that the Epicurean sage can do without: 'if there are no golden statues of youths through the house, holding fiery lamps in their right hands to light the night-time feasts' (De Rerum Natura 2.24-6). Thus the Homeric palace became, in Latin, an emblem of wealth contrasted with simple contentment.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.91-100

anchor: leaves of a tall poplar tree
title: The weaving women
greek: οἷά τε φύλλα μακεδνῆς αἰγείροιο (hoia te phulla makednēs aigeiroio)
short: Fifty serving women grind corn and spin, their hands moving 'like the leaves of a tall poplar'; the next line on dripping oil is obscure.
body: The simile describes either the constant flickering motion of the spinners' hands or the women themselves seated in rows. Line 7.107, 'from the closely-woven linen the soft olive oil drips down', has puzzled commentators since antiquity: it may mean that the cloth is so closely woven that oil (used to finish linen) runs off it, or that oil drips from the freshly treated material, or simply that it shines. Murray's rendering keeps the literal sense. The passage closes with a pointed parallel: as Phaeacian men excel in seafaring, their women excel at the loom, by Athena's gift (7.108-11). The fifty slave-women equal the number in Odysseus' own house (22.421), a quiet link between the two households.

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 7.105-7

anchor: a great orchard of four acres
title: The garden of Alcinous
greek: ἔκτοσθεν δ᾽ αὐλῆς μέγας ὄρχατος ἄγχι θυράων / τετράγυος (ektosthen d' aulēs megas orchatos anchi thuraōn / tetraguos)
short: Alcinous' orchard, vineyard and gardens bear fruit all the year round, ripening in endless succession under the west wind: a paradise on earth.
body: The orchard contains pears, pomegranates, apples, figs and olives whose fruit 'perishes not nor fails in winter or in summer', 'pear upon pear ... fig upon fig', while the vineyard simultaneously shows every stage of the vintage. This is the condition of the Golden Age and of Elysium, where the west wind always blows (4.563-8), and it is sustained by two springs, one of which serves the townsfolk too. Merry cites Bothe's gloss of orchatos as a garden formed of rows of trees. The garden became a byword: Milton names the 'gardens ... of renowned Alcinous' among the paradises surpassed by Eden (Paradise Lost 9.439-41). Within the Odyssey it contrasts with the real, laborious orchard of Laertes on Ithaca, where Odysseus proves his identity by naming the trees his father gave him (24.336-44).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.112

anchor: pour the wine last of all
title: The last libation to Hermes
greek: οἳ δέπασσιν σπένδοντας ἐϋσκόπῳ Ἀργεϊφόντῃ, / ᾧ πυμάτῳ σπένδεσκον, ὅτε μνησαίατο κοίτου (hoi depassin spendontas euskopōi Argeiphontēi, / hōi pumatōi spendeskon, hote mnēsaiato koitou)
short: Odysseus arrives as the Phaeacians pour the evening's final libation to Hermes before going to bed.
body: A libation (spondē) was a portion of wine poured on the ground or into the fire for a god before drinking; Greek feasts began and ended with them. The last libation of the night went to Hermes, apparently as the god of sleep and dreams who closes the eyes of men with his wand (5.47-8). Merry, in his note on 7.138, reports Nitzsch's objection that Hermes' wand is not the symbol of natural sleep, so the exact reason for the custom remains uncertain. The timing is dramatic: Odysseus enters at the very moment the feast is closing, and the hush that falls as he appears from the mist (7.144-5) interrupts a ritual. The Phaeacians' piety is part of their fitness as hosts.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.138

anchor: on the hearth in the ashes
title: The suppliant at the hearth
greek: κὰδ δ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἐπ᾽ ἐσχάρῃ ἕζετ᾽ ἐν κονίῃσιν (kad d' ar' ep' escharēi hezet' en koniēisin)
short: After clasping Arete's knees, Odysseus sits in the ashes of the hearth, the holiest place in the house, in the suppliant's posture.
body: Merry: 'He sits in the posture of a suppliant.' The hearth (eschara or hestia) was the religious centre of the household, and to sit there in the ashes was to claim the protection of the family and its gods while expressing utter humiliation. The most famous historical example is Themistocles, who, fleeing Athens, sat at the hearth of the Molossian king Admetus holding the king's son, and so obtained protection (Thucydides 1.136-7). The silence that follows (7.154) is tense: the Phaeacians do not know how to respond until the old Echeneus reminds Alcinous of his duty. Raising the suppliant from the hearth and seating him on a chair, as Alcinous then does (7.167-9), is the act of acceptance.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.153
J. Gould, 'Hiketeia', Journal of Hellenic Studies 93 (1973) 74-103

title: Echeneus, the wise elder
greek: Ἐχένηος (Echenēos)
short: Echeneus, 'Ship-holder', the eldest of the Phaeacians, breaks the silence and reminds Alcinous to treat the suppliant properly.
body: Echeneus' name, like most Phaeacian names, comes from seafaring (echein, 'hold', and naus, 'ship'). The wise old counsellor who speaks when others are silent is a familiar figure: Nestor in the Iliad, Halitherses and Mentor in Odyssey II. His rebuke is gentle but pointed, 'this is not the better way, nor is it seemly', and shows the Phaeacians' respect for traditional law and for age. He appears again at 11.342-6, where he endorses Arete's proposal of more gifts and defers to Alcinous.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.155
J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 7.155

title: Zeus, protector of suppliants
greek: Διὶ τερπικεραύνῳ ... ὅς θ᾽ ἱκέτῃσιν ἅμ᾽ αἰδοίοισιν ὀπηδεῖ (Dii terpikeraunōi ... hos th' hiketēisin ham' aidoioisin opēdei)
short: Zeus 'attends upon reverend suppliants': the suppliant is aidoios, one to be treated with awe, because Zeus walks beside him.
body: The couplet, spoken by Echeneus and repeated by Alcinous (7.180-1), expresses Zeus' role as Hikesios, the guardian of suppliants, as Nausicaa had named him guardian of strangers and beggars (6.207-8). The adjective aidoios, 'reverend, to be respected', is the passive counterpart of aidōs: the suppliant inspires the respectful restraint that aidōs implies. Odysseus had applied the same word to himself when he prayed to the river (5.447). The libation to Zeus that follows ratifies the guest's acceptance. In Book IX the Cyclops will mock exactly this principle, saying that the Cyclopes care nothing for Zeus (9.269-78).

sources.cite: J. B. Hainsworth, commentary on Books V-VIII in A. Heubeck, S. West and J. B. Hainsworth, A Commentary on Homer's Odyssey, vol. I (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1988), note on 7.164-5

title: Pontonous the herald
greek: Ποντόνοος (Pontonoos)
short: The herald Pontonous, 'Sea-minded', mixes the wine; heralds in Homer serve at feasts and sacrifices as well as carrying messages.
body: The name, from pontos, 'sea', and noos, 'mind', is another of the speaking nautical names of Scheria. Heralds (kērukes) were respected public servants under the protection of Zeus and Hermes: they summoned assemblies, carried the speaker's staff, poured libations and served at banquets. Pontonous also guides the blind Demodocus to his chair and hangs his lyre where he can reach it (8.62-9, 8.105-7). The mixing of the bowl, krater, was the formal preliminary to drinking: wine was always mixed with water, and the first drops poured as libation (7.183).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 8.111-19

title: The Spinners (Klōthes)
greek: ἅσσα οἱ Αἶσα Κατὰ Κλῶθές τε βαρεῖαι / γεινομένῳ νήσαντο λίνῳ (hassa hoi Aisa Kata Klōthes te bareiai / geinomenōi nēsanto linōi)
short: Alcinous says that once home Odysseus must suffer what Fate (Aisa) and the 'heavy Spinners' spun for him at birth.
body: The image of fate as a thread spun at birth is common in Homer, usually with Moira or Aisa as spinner (Il. 20.127-8, 24.209-10) or the gods as a whole (Od. 1.17, 8.579). Only here are the Klōthes, 'Spinners', named as a group; later tradition personified them as the three Fates, Clotho, Lachesis and Atropos (Hesiod, Theogony 905). Merry calls them the half-personified agency of aisa. Alcinous' words are ominous though he does not know it: the Phaeacians will deliver Odysseus safely, but what awaits him in Ithaca is the struggle with the suitors and the further wandering foretold by Tiresias (11.119-37).

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.197

title: Gods seen face to face
greek: αἰεὶ γὰρ τὸ πάρος γε θεοὶ φαίνονται ἐναργεῖς (aiei gar to paros ge theoi phainontai enargeis)
short: Alcinous wonders whether the stranger is a god, for the gods visit the Phaeacians openly, feasting beside them at their sacrifices.
body: Enargēs means 'visible, in bodily presence'. Elsewhere Homer stresses how dangerous such visibility is: 'the gods are hard to look on when they appear in manifest form' (Il. 20.131), and they usually appear in disguise, as Athena does throughout these books. The Phaeacians' privilege links them with the age of heroes and with the Ethiopians, at whose feasts the gods are guests (Il. 1.423-4; Od. 1.22-6). There is dramatic irony here: Athena has just been walking among them unrecognised. Alcinous adds that the Phaeacians are close to the gods 'as are the Cyclopes and the wild tribes of the Giants', a comparison that hints at the dangers of such closeness. Odysseus' modest denial, 'I am not like the immortals', is both truthful and politic.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.201

title: The shameless belly (gastēr)
greek: οὐ γάρ τι στυγερῇ ἐπὶ γαστέρι κύντερον ἄλλο (ou gar ti stugerēi epi gasteri kunteron allo)
short: Odysseus asks to eat despite his grief: nothing is more shameless than the 'hateful belly', which forces a man to remember it.
body: Kunteros, literally 'more doglike', is the strongest Homeric word for shamelessness; Merry renders the thought: 'there never was anything more shameless than' the belly. The belly (gastēr) is a recurrent theme of the Odyssey. Odysseus returns to it as a beggar (15.344, 17.286-9, 18.53-4), and hunger drives men to crime, wandering and humiliation. The belly is a marker of mortality: Odysseus, unlike Akhilleus, accepts the body's needs as part of the human condition, while gods eat ambrosia and need nothing. The speech is also tactically clever: it is a polite way of declining to answer questions until he has been fed.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.216

title: Arete's question
greek: τίς πόθεν εἰς ἀνδρῶν; τίς τοι τάδε εἵματ᾽ ἔδωκεν; (tis pothen eis andrōn? tis toi tade heimat' edōken?)
short: Arete recognises the clothes she made herself and asks the stranger who he is and who gave them to him.
body: The first half of her question is the standard formula of hospitality, asked of a guest after he has eaten (cf. 1.170, 10.325). The second is pointed: the clothes betray a connection with her daughter, and a queen must know how a strange man came by them. Odysseus' answer (7.241-97) is a model of tact. He gives a truthful account of Calypso, the storm and his landing, but omits his name (which he will not reveal until 9.19-20) and praises Nausicaa's good sense, taking on himself the blame for not entering the city with her. Clothing is a means of recognition throughout the poem (19.215-60, where Penelope tests the beggar by asking about Odysseus' clothes).

title: Aisima: due measure
greek: ἀμείνω δ᾽ αἴσιμα πάντα (ameinō d' aisima panta)
short: Alcinous declares that 'fair measure in all things is best': he will not be angry without cause.
body: Aisimos means 'according to aisa', one's proper share or lot, and so 'fitting, right, in due measure'. Merry renders the line 'fair measure in all things is best'. The maxim is an early ancestor of the Greek ideal of moderation, later summed up in the Delphic 'nothing in excess' (mēden agan). Alcinous says it in reply to Odysseus' tactful claim that men are 'quick to anger' (7.307), and it characterises the Phaeacian king as reasonable. The same line is spoken by Menelaus to Telemachus (15.71), where Menelaus too is refusing to detain a guest. The vocabulary connects courtesy with the larger idea of a world ordered by allotted portions.

sources.cite: W. W. Merry and J. Riddell, Homer's Odyssey, vol. I: Books I-XII (2nd ed., Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1886), note on 7.310

anchor: wouldst have my daughter to wife
title: Alcinous offers his daughter
greek: παῖδά τ᾽ ἐμὴν ἐχέμεν καὶ ἐμὸς γαμβρὸς καλέεσθαι (paida t' emēn echemen kai emos gambros kaleesthai)
short: Without knowing his name, Alcinous wishes that the stranger would marry Nausicaa and stay, but promises not to keep him against his will.
body: The offer is remarkable: a king offers his daughter, with a house and property, to a nameless foreigner on the strength of a single evening. It answers Nausicaa's own wish (6.244-5) and fits a widespread folk-tale pattern in which a shipwrecked stranger wins the king's daughter. The poem raises the possibility only to set it aside; Odysseus does not respond, but prays that Alcinous will fulfil his promise of convoy (7.331-3). Scholars have noted that Scheria offers Odysseus a third alternative home, after Calypso's island, which he again declines. Alcinous' tact, 'against thy will shall no one of the Phaeacians keep thee', contrasts with Calypso, who kept him 'perforce'.

title: Rhadamanthus' journey to Tityus in Euboea
greek: ξανθὸν Ῥαδάμανθυν / ἦγον ἐποψόμενον Τιτυὸν Γαιήϊον υἱόν (xanthon Rhadamanthun / ēgon epopsomenon Tituon Gaiēion huion)
short: Alcinous boasts that Phaeacian ships once carried Rhadamanthus to visit the giant Tityus in Euboea, 'the furthest of lands', and back in a day.
body: The allusion is to a myth not otherwise known. Rhadamanthus, brother of Minos, lives in Elysium, at the end of the earth (4.563-4); Tityus, a son of Earth (Gaia), assaulted Leto and was punished in Hades, where Odysseus will see him stretched over nine acres while vultures tear his liver (11.576-81). Why Rhadamanthus, a just judge, visited him is unclear; one suggestion is that he went to see or judge him. Calling Euboea, which lies close to mainland Greece, the 'furthest' of lands shows how the Phaeacians see the world from their remote western position: for them the Greek heartland is the edge of the map.
